The symbols themselves are set in a legacy 8-bit IPA Kiel font with no Unicode mapping, so they could not be read as text, and the PDF could not be rendered (no PDF renderer available; the in-app browser offered it as a download). For the symbols, names, numbers, codepoints and examples I used the IPA's own text transcription: its interactive chart (IPA_charts_TI.html, DIACRITICS table) and the data file behind it (IPA_charts_TI/dbs/arrays.js), which gives for each diacritic the IPA name, IPA number, Unicode name and codepoint, and linked examples. Every codepoint and Unicode name was checked against unicode.org UnicodeData.txt (Unicode 18.0.0).

The PDF text layer is in a legacy font encoding (the stress example comes out as garbage such as '®foUn«"tIS«n'), so the labels were taken from the text layer and the symbols themselves from the rendered page image. Codepoints were then fixed from the Unicode 18.0 code charts (Spacing Modifier Letters, Combining Diacritical Marks, General Punctuation, C0 Controls and Basic Latin) and from the raw wikitext of Wikipedia's 'IPA number' article, whose prosody table encodes the nine marks as U+02C8, U+02CC, U+02D0, U+02D1, U+0306, U+002E, U+007C, U+2016 and U+203F. Python's unicodedata (UCD 13.0) gave the same character names.

engine_today_means.already: letters: at least one of seven IBM modules (enus, engb, dede, eses, esus, frfr, itit: the ones whose phones engine/espeak_phonemes.py gives an IPA value for) has the sound as a phone of its own; frca, jajp and plpl were not consulted, so a sound only they have is under-reported. marks: the modules do it themselves.
engine_today_means.partly: letters: no module has it; the shipped packs say it as another module phone, reshaped by the accent layer, made by the accent layer, or as it is (a plain substitution). marks: a mechanism covers some cases, or some sounds so marked are defined one by one.
engine_today_means.absent: nothing in the shipped product says it.

symbols.chart_example: p’ (Bilabial), t’ (Dental/alveolar), k’ (Velar), s’ (Alveolar fricative); correctly encoded pʼ tʼ kʼ sʼ = U+0070 U+02BC, U+0074 U+02BC, U+006B U+02BC, U+0073 U+02BC
symbols.articulatory: ejective: the consonant it follows is made with a glottalic egressive airstream; the glottis is closed and the larynx raised during the oral closure, compressing the air in the mouth and pharynx, which escapes at the oral release

acoustic_correlates.text: on stops: a release burst followed by a gap (the glottal closure is still held) before voicing starts, so voice onset is delayed relative to a plain unaspirated stop but with no aspiration noise; ejectives in Tsova-Tush had shorter VOT than the aspirated stops they contrast with

two typological patterns (Lindau 1984; Kingston 1985, 2005, as summarised by Kye): 'stiff' ejectives with long VOT, intense burst, raised f0 and modal or tense voice at the vowel onset, and fast amplitude rise; 'slack' ejectives with short VOT, ordinary burst, lowered f0, creaky vowel onset and slow amplitude rise; languages and speakers mix these properties
creakier voice quality (lower spectral tilt, H1*-H2*) at the onset of the following vowel and an f0 difference compared with aspirated stops, with marked differences between speakers

often described as 'spat' or popping consonants, but may be weak and easy to mistake for plain stops; on fricatives (the chart's s’) the oral pressure leaks out during the frication, so the ejective quality is less salient

symbols.notes: Printed alone at the head of the chart's Ejectives column, followed by 'Examples:' p’ Bilabial, t’ Dental/alveolar, k’ Velar, s’ Alveolar fricative. The four examples are NOT separate entries (example combinations of pulmonic letters with this mark); their base letters belong to the pulmonic section. The chart's glyph looks like a curly right quotation mark, but the IPA ejective is U+02BC; do not encode it as U+0027 APOSTROPHE or U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK (Unicode notes U+2019 is the preferred punctuation apostrophe and annotates U+02BC 'glottal stop, glottalization, ejective'). IPA number 401 comes from Wikipedia's IPA number page (4nn = segmental diacritic). features.place: labial-velar (double articulation: lips rounded and tongue back raised toward the soft palate)

acoustic_correlates.text: No voicing: the segment is a stretch of aperiodic noise with no harmonics and no voice bar; whatever formant structure shows comes from noise passing through a [w]-shaped tract.

The tract shape is that of [w]: a labial and a velar constriction, like a close back rounded vowel; rounding at the lips lowers all formants, so the noise energy is concentrated low in the spectrum, with low F1 and low F2 shapes visible in the following vowel's onset transitions.

In English 'wh' words the sound is often realised as a voiceless approximant [w̥], a labialised glottal fricative [hʷ] or an [hw] sequence rather than strong velar friction, so the noise is typically weak and breathy rather than sibilant-like.

symbols.notes: Redefined in 1979 from 'voiceless w' to a fricative with the place of k͡p (per the Wikipedia article); whether it is a fricative or an approximant is disputed.

features.manner: lateral flap (single ballistic contact, air escaping over the sides of the tongue)

acoustic_correlates.text: A single quick contact of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, with airflow over the sides of the tongue instead of the centre: acoustically a very brief lateral interval rather than a sustained [l].
During the lateral contact the spectrum should resemble a lateral: low F1, a relatively high F3, and antiformants from the pocket of air above the tongue acting as a side branch.

Duration is of the order of a tap (a few tens of milliseconds), much shorter than [l]; many languages described with a lateral flap actually have a flap indeterminate between central and lateral, so [ɾ]-like tokens are expected.

symbols.notes: Approved in 1928 and redefined as an alveolar lateral flap in 1979 (per the Wikipedia article). Wikipedia also notes that some 'lateral flaps' are central/lateral-indeterminate (e.g. Japanese).

symbols.articulatory: Marks the syllable that carries the word's main stress. The mark is written before the stressed syllable, not before its vowel.

acoustic_correlates.text: Longer syllable. symbols.articulatory: global rise: intonation, not lexical tone; the whole prosodic unit (when attached to a boundary mark such as ‖) or the marked word/syllable has rising overall pitch

features.form: arrow placed before the word/syllable or with a boundary mark

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 rises over the span it applies to (the pitch trend over the intonation unit is upward rather than declining); in English it typically marks yes-no questions or non-final list items, the rise realised mainly on and after the marked syllable.
Being superimposed on lexical tones in a tone language, it shifts and tilts the tone targets rather than replacing them; the raised end is relative to the speaker's range.

features.form: arrow placed before the word/syllable or with a boundary mark

acoustic_correlates.text: F0 falls over the span it applies to; in English a fall on the last prominent syllable typically marks statements and wh-questions, realised as a down-glide on that syllable if it is final or a step down to the following syllables otherwise.
Chunks with gradually declining pitch are the most common prosodic contours; F0 resets upward at the start of the next chunk.

Phrase-level declination itself is small in tone languages (about 0.25 semitone between adjacent high tones in all-high Mandarin sentences), so a marked global fall should be clearly larger than plain declination.

problems.problem: The full chart PDF could not be read as text; the inventory comes from visually reading the official 600 ppi PNG of the pulmonic sub-chart (cross-checked against the Wikipedia 'IPA number' table, which matches symbol for symbol).

IPA names come from the wazu.jp test page (2012, quoting Handbook names), not from the Handbook itself, which was not opened. That page has typos ('Truned R, right tail', 'Small capitial L', corrected here) and wrongly labels looptail g #210 as U+026D (U+026D is L WITH RETROFLEX HOOK; looptail g is U+0067). ⱱ (#184) is not on that page; its name 'right-hook v' comes from Wikipedia.
The Oxford and Manitoba course pages show no author, date or licence in the fetched text; author attributions are inferred from the URL paths.

No fetched source gave acoustic figures for palatal, uvular, pharyngeal, glottal-stop, tap/flap, labiodental-flap, lateral-fricative, j, ɰ, ʎ or ʟ articulations; those correlates are described in words and tagged recalled-unverified. No tap/flap or trill durations or rates in Hz were found, so none are given.
Hz figures that are given (bursts, nasal resonances, sibilant peaks, lateral F2) are from a single page about English and should be treated as typical values, not targets.
Unicode licence recorded from the UCD ReadMe's pointer to the terms of use; the licence text itself was not opened.

The official IPA_Kiel.pdf could not be read as text (no PDF renderer here; the fetch tool would not transcribe it). The section was read from the IPA's official 600 ppi PNG of the non-pulmonic box, viewed as an image; the transcription is mine, from that image.

Wikipedia's 'International Phonetic Alphabet chart' says it shows 'the official IPA chart, revised to 2020' but its non-pulmonic table is an expanded one (ᶑ, voiceless implosives, ejective affricates, click combinations, ʞ). The IPA's own page says the 2020 issue was identical to the 2015/2005 revision, and the current 2026 issue still says 'revised to 2015/2005'. The official box was followed.

Official symbol names (Handbook of the IPA, 1999) could not be checked; the Handbook was not available. ipa_name values come from Wikipedia's naming-conventions page (bull's eye, pipe, exclamation mark, double pipe, hook-top b, hook-top d) and are null for ǂ ʄ ɠ ʛ ʼ; names recalled for those are in notes and tagged recalled-unverified.
IPA numbers come from Wikipedia's 'IPA number' page (a secondary source), not from the Handbook's Appendix 2.

Unicode character names disagree with the IPA labels: U+01C3 is named LATIN LETTER RETROFLEX CLICK but is the IPA (post)alveolar click; U+01C2 is named LATIN LETTER ALVEOLAR CLICK but is the IPA palatoalveolar click (Unicode's own annotations say so). Do not map by Unicode name.
The chart prints the ejective mark with a glyph that looks like a typographic right single quote; the correct character is U+02BC, not U+2019 or U+0027.

Miller & Shah 2009 contradicts itself: the introduction says the dental and palatal click bursts are shorter, while the results and discussion say the dental and lateral bursts are longer than the alveolar and palatal ones. The results/discussion version was used. The click letters in that PDF are in a private font and were identified from context; the order of Traill's intensity scale is therefore only partly certain (only 'click bursts above pulmonic t, k, q' was used).

No fetched source gave acoustic measurements for the bilabial click ʘ, or Hz/ms values for implosives or ejectives (only Nihalani's pressure values in cm H2O). Place-specific formant-transition statements for the implosives and the 'rising voicing amplitude during closure' of implosives are tagged recalled-unverified (the latter appeared only in a search-result snippet, not in a fetched page).
Ejective acoustics vary across languages and speakers (stiff vs slack types, mixed patterns); there is no single acoustic target for ʼ.
Lindau (1984), Kingston (1985, 2005), Ladefoged & Traill (1994) and Traill (1997) are cited only second-hand through the papers that were read.
The Unicode PDF code charts (U0180, U0250, U02B0) were downloaded but could not be read as text; NamesList.txt 18.0.0 was used for codepoints and names instead.
The chart carries no revision date beyond 'IPA Chart revised to 2015/2005'; the copy read is the 2026 annual re-issue ((c) 2026 IPA). No symbol-level change since 2015 was found.
ʢ: the chart label says 'Voiced epiglottal fricative' but the IPA's own symbol list names it 'VOICED EPIGLOTTAL FRICATIVE/APPROXIMANT'.

ʡ: the chart says only 'Epiglottal plosive' (no voicing); the Unicode NamesList annotates U+02A1 as 'voiced epiglottal stop'; Wikipedia describes it as voiceless and says a voiced one may be impossible.

ɧ: the chart defines it as 'Simultaneous ʃ and x', the IPA symbol list as 'voiceless postalveolar-velar fricative', Unicode as 'coarticulated velar and palatoalveolar fricative'; phoneticians (Ladefoged and Maddieson, via Wikipedia) doubt that double friction occurs, and real Swedish realisations vary. Not checked in Ladefoged and Maddieson directly.
ʍ: fricative vs approximant status is disputed (Wikipedia reports the IPA Handbook calls it both); the Handbook itself was not opened.

Bottom tie bar: the number chart and symbol list give it '(509)' in parentheses, the number of 'Linking' ‿ U+203F UNDERTIE; the symbol list also gives both the same AFII code 230F. Recorded here as 509 with U+035C; the suprasegmentals helper should keep U+203F as a separate character.

Esling (1996, via the Wikipedia article for 2010) treats epiglottals as pharyngeal manners, not a separate place, whereas the chart lists them as epiglottal; features record the chart's place and note Esling's view.
The IPA symbol list abbreviates Unicode names ('W/' for 'WITH'); the unicode_name values here are the full names from UnicodeData.txt 18.0.0.

No fetched source gives hertz or millisecond values for ʍ, w, ɥ, ʜ, ʢ, ʡ, ʑ, ɺ or ɧ; those correlates are described in words and the unsupported ones are tagged recalled-unverified. Attempts that failed: Macquarie University 'approximants.pdf' returned 403; an ICPhS 2023 Swedish sj-sound paper URL returned 404.

The [ɕ] centre-of-gravity ranges were read off the plotted figures of Żygis and Hamann (2003) for one female speaker; their male speaker showed overlap between [ɕ], [ʃʲ] and [ʂ], so these ranges are not general norms.
Esling (1996): the PDF text layer garbles several phonetic symbols in its Table 1; the symbol-to-description pairing was taken from the rendered page image.
UNC LING 520 outline: author name and year are not printed in the file; attributed to the course URL only.

The full official chart PDF (IPA_Kiel.pdf) could not be read as text here (no PDF renderer); the vowel section was read from the official sub-chart PNG plus the IPA's own tooltip-chart data file, which agree.

Revision naming: the printed chart says 'IPA Chart revised to 2015/2005' with copyright year 2026; earlier issues were labelled 2018 and 2020 but are the same revision. The brief's '2015 chart as revised' is that revision.

Formant numbers are secondary: Catford (2001) values were read only as quoted on Wikipedia 'Formant' (male voice, 16 of 28 vowels, F1/F2 only), and Peterson & Barney (1952) values only as quoted on a Princeton course page (American English men, 9 vowels mapped by me from ASCII labels: /e/ 'bet' -> ɛ, /a/ 'father' -> ɑ, /aw/ 'bought' -> ɔ, /L/ 'but' -> ʌ, /U/ 'book' -> ʊ, /ae/ 'bat' -> æ, /I/ 'bit' -> ɪ). The P&B vowels are English phonemes, not cardinal qualities (e.g. American 'but' is more central than cardinal ʌ).

No fetched source gave hertz values for ɨ ʉ ʏ ɘ ɵ ɜ ɞ ɐ (or F3 for most vowels); those carry relational correlates only. Attempts to open sources with cardinal-vowel formants of Daniel Jones (Vaissière 2011, HAL) were blocked by an access-denied page, and Jassem & Krzyśko 1992 'In quest for Cardinal Vowels' (Archives of Acoustics) full text could not be read.

Wikipedia 'Phonetic symbols in Unicode' was fetched but the tool's summary returned wrong character names (e.g. 'LATIN LETTER REVERSED I' for U+0268); it was discarded and names were taken from unicode.org UnicodeData.txt and the IPA's own data instead.
ə and ɐ: the IPA descriptions ('mid central vowel', 'near-open central vowel') give no rounding value; features.rounding is 'unspecified'.

The relational F1/F2/F3 statements per vowel are my own application of the general rules in wiki_formant, wiki_vowel and umanitoba_formants (height ~ inverse F1, backness ~ F2, rounding lowers F2/F3 in front vowels and F1/F2 in back vowels); the specific neighbour-by-neighbour orderings (e.g. ɶ having a small rounding effect, ɯ F2 drifting toward central) are inferences, not quoted findings.

Confusable code points named in notes (U+0131, U+0263, U+0269, U+0277, U+029A, U+01DD, U+03B1, U+03B5, U+03C5, U+2205 etc.) were checked against Python's local unicodedata (Unicode 13.0) only, not a fetched page; U+0131/U+0269/U+0277/U+029A as retired IPA letters come from wiki_ipa_number.
Cardinal-vowel numbers in notes (CV1-16) are recalled-unverified; no fetched source in this session lists them.

The official PDF (IPA_Kiel.pdf) could not be read glyph by glyph: its symbols use a legacy 8-bit IPA Kiel font with no Unicode mapping and no PDF renderer was available. The symbol list, names, numbers and examples come from the IPA's own interactive (text) chart and its data file; the revision, licence and the descender note were read from the PDF itself.
Trying to open the PDF in the in-app browser made the site serve it as a download, so a save dialog was shown to the user; nothing was saved by this helper through that dialog.

Examples: the interactive chart data lists more examples than the printed chart probably shows (e.g. ᵰ ᵭ ꭨ for the tilde overlay, m̩ for syllabic, b̤a̤ / b̰a̰, o˞ and ɝ for rhoticity, p̚). Which ones the printed PDF shows was not verified; chart_example gives the main ones.

The IPA data encodes the 'Retracted' example e̠ as e + U+0331 COMBINING MACRON BELOW, but gives U+0320 COMBINING MINUS SIGN BELOW as the diacritic. This file uses U+0320 for the diacritic, as the IPA's own codepoint field gives.

The interactive chart HTML shows 'Nasalized' with U+0342 COMBINING GREEK PERISPOMENI (a display workaround) while its data gives U+0303 COMBINING TILDE; this file uses U+0303. Its display strings also contain U+25CC DOTTED CIRCLE and U+034F COMBINING GRAPHEME JOINER as layout aids; neither is part of any diacritic.

Descender alternates: only the over-ring (ŋ̊, U+030A) is printed on the chart. The syllabic over-stroke U+030D (e.g. ŋ̍, described by Wikipedia) and the non-syllabic arch above U+0311 are not printed, so they are not counted; the merge step may want them as unofficial alternates.
U+02E4 (IPA pharyngealized) is easily confused with U+02C1 MODIFIER LETTER REVERSED GLOTTAL STOP; only U+02E4 is IPA.

Many correlates are recalled-unverified because no fetched source gave them: voiceless sonorants, palatalized (raised F2), velarized (lowered F2), linguolabial, dental/apical/laminal spectra, the F1 direction for ATR/RTR, syllabic/non-syllabic duration and intensity, nasal pole-zero pairs, and raised/lowered consonant frication. They should be checked against a phonetics text such as Ladefoged & Maddieson, The Sounds of the World's Languages, or Stevens, Acoustic Phonetics, before use.

The Laboratory Phonology article (altamimi2017) is open access, but its licence line was not found in the fetched page text; the three ICPhS/ASA papers carry no licence statement. Only the facts are used, in our own words.

The attribution text in the 2026 PDF names a path containing '_next_year' (…/pdfs_IPA_charts_E/_next_year/IPA_Kiel.pdf), which differs from the URL that was downloaded; the revision line still reads 2015/2005.

Breathy and creaky H1-H2 directions come from cross-language studies; actual values vary by language and speaker (keating2011 found the same-named phonation types differ across languages). No hertz or millisecond targets are given for phonation diacritics.

The official chart PDF uses a legacy-encoded font, so codepoints cannot be read from it. Symbol identity was read from the rendered image, and codepoints come from glyph identity, the Unicode 18.0 charts and the Wikipedia IPA number wikitext. Unicode itself gives IPA annotations only for ˈ ˌ ː ˑ (and '= short' for U+0306). For . | ‖ ‿, the IPA meaning rests on the chart label plus Wikipedia, not on Unicode.

Revision disagreement: the IPA site and the 2026 chart say 'revised to 2015/2005' (re-issued every year since 2025), while Wikipedia's International Phonetic Alphabet article calls the official summary chart 'revised in 2020'.

The 1999 Handbook of the IPA was not opened. IPA numbers 501-509 and the official meaning of minor (foot) group, major (intonation) group and linking are taken from the chart labels and from Wikipedia (which cites the Handbook).

Wikipedia's IPA number table gives 509 both to the linking undertie ‿ (U+203F) and to the lower tie bar ͜ (U+035C, Other symbols). Whether they really share a number is unverified; the other_symbols helper should check.

No fetched source measures the IPA 'minor (foot) group' or 'major (intonation) group' as such. The numbers are for ToBI break 3 (intermediate phrase) and break 4 (intonation phrase) in English and Mandarin radio news, and German news. Equating the IPA groups with these categories is an assumption.

No fetched source gives a duration ratio for half-long (ˑ) or extra-short (breve) as such. The half-long evidence is the Finnish description and Estonian second-syllable vowel durations, and reading those as half-long is an inference. Extra-short has no numbers.
Secondary stress has no fetched acoustic measurements; its correlates are recalled-unverified.

The stress sources disagree on F0 and intensity: Sluijter and van Heuven find that F0 and overall intensity cue pitch accent, not stress, while Guo reports a stressed/unstressed F0 ratio of 1.13 for citation-form English words, where stress and accent are confounded.
Fuchs (2015) was read only as the Interspeech abstract page, not the full paper.
Licences of the conference papers (ISCA/ICPhS) are not stated on the copies read. The JEFUL article licence was not checked.
NFC normalisation turns the chart example e + U+0306 into the precomposed U+0115 (ĕ). The engine will meet both forms.
Arguable membership: Global rise ↗ and Global fall ↘ have IPA numbers 510-511 in the same 500 prosody series but are printed in the Tones and word accents box, so they are left to the tones helper.

Rising-falling tone letter: the IPA's own symbol list gives 02E7 + 02E6 + 02E8 (˧˦˨, levels 3-4-2), and pixel measurement of the Doulos SIL and DejaVu Sans sub-chart images agrees (start 3, peak 4, end near 2), as does Wikipedia's IPA article ('since the 2018 revision'). The IPA Kiel-font image (the Association's recommended chart) draws a ligature whose end meets the stave nearer level 3 (˧˦˧). Recorded ˧˦˨; the Kiel glyph may be a font drawing difference.

Wikipedia's 'IPA number' article lists 533 as ˨˦˨ (2-4-2) and Wikipedia's IPA article says the 1999 Handbook chart had ˦˥˦; both differ from the current IPA list (˧˦˨). The Handbook itself was not opened.

The IPA symbol list's TIPA codes disagree with its own hex values for three contour letters: high rising \tone{45} vs 02E7+02E5 (35), low rising \tone{12} vs 02E9+02E7 (13), rising-falling \tone{454} vs 02E7+02E6+02E8 (342). The hex values, the chart images and Wikipedia agree, so the hex values were used.

Contour tone letters have no code points of their own; they are sequences of U+02E5..U+02E9 that fonts ligate. The Doulos chart PDF's text layer maps them to U+FFFD, so the sequences come from the IPA symbol list and image measurement, not from extractable chart text.

equivalent_to pairs each diacritic with the tone letter printed in the same chart row, as the brief asks. The Handbook (as quoted by Wikipedia, not opened) says this pairing is only a layout simplification: diacritics have at most doubled marks for extra high/low and coarse H/M/L contour points, letters have five levels. A synthesiser should not treat é as exactly ˦ or ě as exactly ˩˥.

Downstep and upstep: the chart images show plain-looking arrows. The IPA symbol list and the Doulos text layer identify them as U+A71C and U+A71B (raised modifier arrows). U+2193/U+2191 and the raised exclamation marks U+A71D/U+A71E are common substitutes in the literature (listed under alt_codepoints) but are not what the chart encodes.
Global rise/fall U+2197/U+2198 have emoji presentation sequences in Unicode 18.0; U+FE0E text style is listed as an alternative, not as the chart's code.

Membership: the section heading is 'Tones and word accents', but no symbol is specific to word accents (pitch accent); all 24 printed symbols are counted. Global rise and fall are intonation marks and downstep and upstep are register shifts, not tones, but the chart prints all four in this section, so they are included here. The word 'or' printed between the first diacritic and letter in the full chart is not an entry.

Hz and ms values come from Mandarin (Xu 1997: eight male Beijing speakers in isolation; Wang et al. 2022: downstep). No fetched source gives absolute F0 values for the IPA's five levels in general; tone levels are relative to the speaker's range. Chao's semitone spacing is taken from Wikipedia's report, not from Chao (1956, 1968) directly. Xu and Sun (2002)'s pitch-rise time formula is quoted from Wang et al. (2022); the original was not opened.

No fetched source gave measurements for extra-high, extra-low, low-rising or rising-falling tones specifically, or for upstep magnitude; those correlates are in words and tagged recalled-unverified or rely on general sources.
